claims.text: The investigated material is equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi (the Cantor alloy).
Fine-grained material has a higher grain-boundary density than coarse-grained material.
The two microstructural states can initially possess similar passive oxide layers under controlled processing.
Annealing at approximately 900°C will produce the fine-grained state, whereas annealing at approximately 1200°C will produce the coarse-grained state.
Sliding wear mechanically disrupts the passive oxide film.
Grain boundaries act as active sites for rapid passive-film repair.
A high grain-boundary density accelerates repassivation after mechanical film disruption.
A low grain-boundary density in coarse-grained material causes slower passive-film reformation.
Slower passive-film reformation prolongs fresh-metal exposure and thereby increases localized corrosion.
Pits in the Cantor alloy preferentially initiate along grain boundaries rather than within grain interiors.
The competition between mechanical passive-film disruption and grain-boundary-assisted repair governs the overall tribo-corrosion degradation rate.
Fine- and coarse-grained specimens will exhibit similar mechanical wear.
The fine-grained specimen will have a significantly lower corrosion contribution than the coarse-grained baseline.
The lower corrosion contribution will reduce total degradation in the fine-grained specimen.
The predicted grain-refinement benefit will hold in moderately corrosive environments that sustain passivity and are controlled by repassivation kinetics.
Very high chloride concentrations or transpassive potentials may negate the benefit of rapid repassivation.
Prior evidence supports enhanced repassivation with increasing grain-boundary density.
The Cantor alloy forms a chromium-associated passive layer that improves corrosion resistance.
Quantitative wear and corrosion contributions under dynamic sliding are not yet fully established.
